latest_release.name: Surya v0.24.0 — Zero-PyTorch Lightweight Architecture, Interactive Web Viewer (surya_gui) & Agent-Ready CLI
latest_release.body:
# Surya v0.24.0 — Zero-PyTorch Lightweight Architecture, Interactive Web Viewer (`surya_gui`) & Agent-Ready CLI

Surya `0.24.0` completes the transition to **Surya 2.5** (`datalab-to/surya-ocr-2.5`) — our 689M-parameter vision-language model for **full-page & per-block OCR**, **layout analysis & reading order**, **inline & block LaTeX math (`<math>`)**, and **HTML table recognition (`<table>` with `colspan` / `rowspan`)** across 90+ languages:

- **85.9 on [OmniParseBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench)** (highest of any open model under 1B parameters) and **83.7% on [olmOCR-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/olmOCR-bench)**.
- **4.5 pages/s on a single H100** at 192 DPI (`6.2 pages/s` at 96 DPI) — **1.7× faster than Surya 2** and **3.2× faster on Apple Silicon (`llama.cpp` Metal)** because compact block headers (`<|Label|><|x0|><|y0|><|x1|><|y1|>`) and compact table tokens cut output tokens per page by **62%**.
- **Zero Heavy ML Dependencies (`pip install surya-ocr` installs in seconds)** — removed `torch`, `torchvision`, `transformers`, `opencv-python-headless`, and `streamlit` from runtime dependencies (`>10,000` lines of legacy v1/RF-DETR code removed). Surya now runs as a lightweight client/orchestrator over **`vllm`** (Docker or Podman), **`llama.cpp`** (`llama-server` / `llama-cli`), or **`mlx-vlm`** (Apple Silicon).
- **New Built-In Interactive Web Viewer (`surya_gui`)** — zero-extra-dependency browser UI to inspect layout boxes, reading order, KaTeX-typeset math, HTML tables, and JSON page by page across all Surya modes.

> Need handwriting, complex forms, or managed VLM parsing at scale with zero infrastructure? Try **[Chandra on the Datalab API](https://www.datalab.to/?utm_source=gh-surya-release)** — get **5,000 free pages every month** when you sign up with a work email.

---

## 1. Built-In Interactive Web Viewer (`surya_gui`)

`surya_gui` now launches a fast, self-contained web viewer directly from the standard library (no `streamlit` installation required):

```bash
surya_gui --port 8000
```

- Drag & drop any **PDF** or **image** (`PNG`, `JPG`, `WEBP`, `GIF`, `TIFF`, `BMP`).
- Switch live between **Full-Page OCR**, **Block OCR** (96 DPI layout + 192 DPI block crops), **Layout**, and **Table Recognition**.
- Interactive SVG overlays for **layout bounding boxes**, **canonical block labels**, and **reading order** with bidirectional hover highlighting between the page canvas and the `Blocks` tab.
- Inspect **Preview** (with live KaTeX math rendering and styled HTML tables), **Blocks**, **HTML**, and **JSON**, with one-click `Copy HTML` and `.json` download.

---

## 2. Clean Top-Level Python API & New Predictor Capabilities

```python
from PIL import Image
from surya import (
    LayoutPredictor,
    RecognitionPredictor,
    SuryaInferenceManager,
    TableRecPredictor,
)

manager = SuryaInferenceManager()  # auto-spawns vllm (GPU) or llama-server (CPU / Apple Silicon)
image = Image.open("page.png").convert("RGB")

# 1. Full-page OCR (default: one VLM call per page -> blocks, bboxes, reading order, HTML + <math>)
rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager)
pages = rec([image])

# Optional: pass skip_labels=[] to also OCR text inside Figure / Picture / Diagram regions
pages_with_figures = rec([image], skip_labels=[])

# 2. Two-stage Layout + Block-mode OCR (auto-runs LayoutPredictor if layouts not passed)
block_pages = rec([image], full_page=False)

# 3. HTML Table Recognition (<table> with colspan / rowspan)
tables = TableRecPredictor(manager)([image])
print(tables[0].html)
```

### What's New in the Predictors & Backends
- **Top-level package exports**: Import `SuryaInferenceManager`, `get_default_manager`, `LayoutPredictor`, `RecognitionPredictor`, `TableRecPredictor`, and `__version__` directly from `surya`.
- **Configurable `skip_labels` (`#544`)**: Pass `skip_labels=[]` (or a custom set of labels) to `RecognitionPredictor` to OCR text inside `Figure`, `Picture`, or `Diagram

Datalab

State of the Art models for Document Intelligence

# Surya Surya is a 689M param document OCR and layout VLM with these features: - Accuracy - scores 85.9 on [OmniParseBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench), the highest of the open models under 1B parameters we have scored, and 83.7% on [olmOCR-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/olmOCR-bench) - Speed - throughput of 4.5 pages/s on one H100 at 192 DPI, 1.7x Surya 2 with MTP (see [Throughput](#throughput)) - Multilingual - scores 74.9% on an internal benchmark set of 91 languages (more [here](#multilingual)) - Layout analysis (`Table`, `Picture`, `SectionHeader`, `Equation`, `Form`, etc.) with reading order and token-count estimates - Tables as HTML (``, ``, `
`, ``) with merged cells as `colspan` / `rowspan` - Zero heavy local ML dependencies - `surya-ocr` is a lightweight client/orchestrator that talks to `vllm` (Docker / Podman), `llama-server` (llama.cpp), or `mlx_vlm.server` (Apple Silicon) ## Try Datalab's Managed Platform Our managed platform uses Surya, our highest accuracy model [Chandra](https://github.com/datalab-to/chandra), and other models. The Datalab API turns documents into verifiable knowledge your agents act on. Every result traces back to its page and position, and one API can parse, extract, fill and edit documents. Get started with **about 5,000 free convert pages every month** (work email) — [sign up](https://www.datalab.to/?utm_source=gh-surya) (takes under 30 seconds) or try our free [public playground](https://www.datalab.to/playground?utm_source=gh-surya). ## Model Information | Layout | OCR | |:------------------------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------:| | | | Surya is named for the [Hindu sun god](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surya), who has universal vision. ## Examples Each row links to annotated views of the same page: OCR, layout, and reading order (Surya 2.5). | Name | Original | OCR | Layout | Order | |-------------------|:-----------------------------------:|------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------:| | Newspaper | [Image](static/images/newspaper.png) | [Image](static/images/newspaper_text.png) | [Image](static/images/newspaper_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/newspaper_reading.png) | | Reference book | [Image](static/images/reference.png) | [Image](static/images/reference_text.png) | [Image](static/images/reference_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/reference_reading.png) | | Math paper | [Image](static/images/math.png) | [Image](static/images/math_text.png) | [Image](static/images/math_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/math_reading.png) | | Government form | [Image](static/images/form.png) | [Image](static/images/form_text.png) | [Image](static/images/form_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/form_reading.png) | | Handwritten letter | [Image](static/images/handwritten.png) | [Image](static/images/handwritten_text.png) | [Image](static/images/handwritten_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/handwritten_reading.png) | | Corporate doc | [Image](static/images/corporate.png) | [Image](static/images/corporate_text.png) | [Image](static/images/corporate_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/corporate_reading.png) | | Japanese tax form | [Image](static/images/japanese.png) | [Image](static/images/japanese_text.png) | [Image](static/images/japanese_layout.png) | [Image](static/images/japanese_reading.png) | The example pages are public pages from [OmniParseBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench). The newspaper (The Alpha, 1881), reference book and math paper are from [olmOCR-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/olmOCR-bench) (Ai2, ODC-BY 1.0). The government form is a US federal form (public domain). The handwritten letter is from the Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Carrie Chapman Catt Papers (public domain). The corporate page is from [ParseBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/llamaindex/ParseBench) (Apache 2.0). The Japanese form is made from a form of the National Tax Agency, Japan, under the Public Data License 1.0: 「国税庁の様式」（国税庁）（https://www.nta.go.jp/）を加工して作成. # Commercial usage The Surya code is licensed under Apache 2.0. The model weights use a modified AI Pubs Open Rail-M license (free for research, personal use, and startups under $5M funding/revenue). For broader commercial licensing of the model weights, visit our pricing page [here](https://www.datalab.to/pricing?utm_source=gh-surya). # Installation Install with: ```shell pip install surya-ocr ``` ## Inference backend prerequisites Surya auto-spawns the inference server on first use, using `vllm` (NVIDIA GPU) or `llama.cpp` (CPU / Apple Silicon): - **NVIDIA GPU:** [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) or [Podman](https://podman.io/) plus the [NVIDIA Container Toolkit](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/cloud-native/container-toolkit/latest/install-guide.html). - **CPU / Apple Silicon:** the `llama-server` binary from llama.cpp: ```shell brew install llama.cpp # macOS # or grab a release from https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases ``` ## Upgrading from Surya v1 If you have v1 code, migrate to `SuryaInferenceManager`: ```python from PIL import Image from surya import SuryaInferenceManager, RecognitionPredictor manager = SuryaInferenceManager() # auto-spawns vllm or llama-server rec = RecognitionPredictor(manager) predictions = rec([Image.open("page.png")]) ``` What's different: - `SuryaInferenceManager` replaces `FoundationPredictor`. The same manager instance is shared across `LayoutPredictor`, `RecognitionPredictor`, and `TableRecPredictor`. - Output schemas return structured `blocks` (with `html`, `label`, `polygon`, `bbox`, `reading_order`, `confidence`); layout boxes include `count` (token budget estimate); table recognition returns full HTML tables (`...
` with `colspan` / `rowspan`). # Usage Surya 2.5 runs layout, OCR, and table recognition through a single VLM. The inference manager spawns a server for you on first use; you can also point it at an existing OpenAI-compatible server via `SURYA_INFERENCE_URL=http://host:port/v1`. - Inspect the settings in `surya/settings.py`. You can override any setting via environment variables (e.g. `SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=vllm`). ### Server lifecycle (`--keep_server`) By default each CLI command spawns the VLM server on startup and shuts it down on exit — so running several commands in a row pays the startup (and, on GPU, the model-load) cost every time. Pass `--keep_server` to leave the server running so later commands attach to it instead of re-spawning: ```shell surya_ocr DATA_PATH --keep_server # spawns the server and leaves it up surya_layout DATA_PATH # attaches to the running server surya_table DATA_PATH # ...and so on, no re-spawn ``` `--keep_server` works on every command. Stop the server when you're done (`docker stop` / `podman stop` the `surya-vllm-*` container, or kill the `llama-server` process), or set `SURYA_INFERENCE_KEEP_ALIVE=1` to make keep-alive the default. ## Interactive App `surya_gui` launches a self-contained interactive web viewer in your browser (with zero extra dependencies) where you can drop PDFs or images and inspect layout boxes, reading order, KaTeX-rendered math, HTML tables, and JSON page by page across all Surya modes (`Full-Page OCR`, `Block OCR`, `Layout`, and `Table Rec`): ```shell surya_gui --port 8000 ``` ## OCR (text recognition) This command writes out a `results.json` file with the detected blocks, labels, bboxes, and HTML content: ```shell surya_ocr DATA_PATH ``` - `DATA_PATH` can be an image, pdf, or folder of images/pdfs - `--stdout` writes the JSON result directly to stdout instead of saving to a directory (ideal for AI agents and shell pipelines) - `--block_mode` runs layout detection first and then OCRs each detected block crop individually (default is single-call full-page OCR) - `--recursive` / `-r` recursively searches subdirectories when `DATA_PATH` is a folder - `--images` will save images of the pages and detected blocks (optional) - `--output_dir` specifies the directory to save results to instead of the default - `--page_range` specifies the page range to process in the PDF, specified as a single number, a comma separated list, a range, or comma separated ranges - example: `0,5-10,20`. - `--keep_server` leaves the inference server running after the command exits so later commands reuse it (see [Server lifecycle](#server-lifecycle---keep_server)). Available on every command. - `--skill` prints the bundled Surya AI agent skill (`SKILL.md`) to stdout; `--install_skill [DIR]` installs it into `.agents/skills/surya/SKILL.md`. The `results.json` file contains a dict keyed by input filename (no extension). Each value is a list of page dicts. Each page dict contains: - `blocks` - per-block OCR results in reading order - `label` - canonicalized layout label (e.g. `Text`, `SectionHeader`, `Table`, `Equation`, `Picture`, `Form`, `PageHeader`, ...). See `surya/layout/label.py:LAYOUT_PRED_RELABEL` for the full canonical-name set. - `raw_label` - original label emitted by the model, before canonicalization - `reading_order` - 0-indexed position in layout output - `html` - block content as HTML (math wrapped in `...`, tables as `...
`, etc.). `""` if the block was skipped - `polygon` - 4-corner polygon in `[[x0,y0],[x1,y0],[x1,y1],[x0,y1]]` order - `bbox` - axis-aligned `[x0, y0, x1, y1]` derived from the polygon - `confidence` - mean per-token probability across the block's decode (0-1) - `skipped` - true if the block was a visual label (e.g. `Picture`) and not OCR'd - `error` - true if the block OCR call failed - `image_bbox` - `[0, 0, width, height]` for the page image **Performance tips** - Throughput is governed by the inference backend. With `vllm`, raise `--max-num-seqs` / `--max-num-batched-tokens` (or `SURYA_INFERENCE_PARALLEL` on the client side) to keep more pages in flight. With `llama.cpp`, set `SURYA_INFERENCE_PARALLEL` to match `--parallel` on `llama-server`. - DPI can also impact throughput significantly - you can adjust `IMAGE_DPI_HIGHRES` to make the right throughput/accuracy tradeoff for your use case. Try going from 192 to 96 for improved throughput. - MTP can also impact latency/throughput. It is turned on automatically only when the checkpoint config declares an MTP head; set `VLLM_ENABLE_MTP=true|false` to override, and `VLLM_MTP_TOKENS` to change the draft length. ### From python ```python from PIL import Image from surya import LayoutPredictor, RecognitionPredictor, SuryaInferenceManager manager = SuryaInferenceManager() recognition_predictor = RecognitionPredictor(manager) # Default: full-page OCR. One VLM call per page. Returns one PageOCRResult per # image: `.blocks` (each with label, html, polygon, bbox, confidence, ...) and # `.image_bbox` — the same schema as block mode. image = Image.open(IMAGE_PATH) predictions = recognition_predictor([image]) # Optional: pass skip_labels=[] to also OCR text inside Figure / Picture / Diagram blocks predictions_all = recognition_predictor([image], skip_labels=[]) # Block mode: pre-run layout (or pass full_page=False to run layout automatically), # then per-block OCR. Same return schema as above. layout = LayoutPredictor(manager) layouts = layout([image]) predictions = recognition_predictor([image], layouts) ``` ## Layout and reading order This command writes out a `results.json` file with the detected layout and reading order: ```shell surya_layout DATA_PATH ``` - `DATA_PATH` can be an image, pdf, or folder of images/pdfs - `--images` will save images of the pages and detected layout boxes (optional) - `--output_dir` specifies the directory to save results to instead of the default - `--page_range` specifies the page range to process in the PDF, specified as a single number, a comma separated list, a range, or comma separated ranges - example: `0,5-10,20`. The `results.json` file contains a dict keyed by input filename (no extension). Each value is a list of page dicts. Each page dict contains: - `bboxes` - layout boxes in reading order - `polygon` - 4-corner polygon `[[x0,y0],[x1,y0],[x1,y1],[x0,y1]]` - `bbox` - axis-aligned `[x0, y0, x1, y1]` derived from the polygon - `label` - canonicalized label. One of `Caption`, `Footnote`, `Equation`, `ListGroup`, `PageHeader`, `PageFooter`, `Picture`, `SectionHeader`, `Table`, `Text`, `Figure`, `Code`, `Form`, `TableOfContents`, `ChemicalBlock`, `Diagram`, `Bibliography`, `BlankPage` - `raw_label` - original label emitted by the model - `position` - 0-indexed reading order - `count` - model's token estimate for OCR'ing this block (rounded to multiples of 50; used to size the per-block decode budget) - `confidence` - mean per-token probability across the layout decode (0-1) - `image_bbox` - `[0, 0, width, height]` - `raw` - raw JSON the layout model emitted, for debugging - `error` - true if the layout call failed ### From python ```python from PIL import Image from surya.inference import SuryaInferenceManager from surya.layout import LayoutPredictor layout_predictor = LayoutPredictor(SuryaInferenceManager()) layout_predictions = layout_predictor([Image.open(IMAGE_PATH)]) ``` ## Table Recognition This command writes out a `results.json` file with each detected table as HTML (with `colspan` / `rowspan` for merged cells). For full document conversion to Markdown, JSON, HTML, or RAG chunks, check out [Marker](https://github.com/datalab-to/marker). ```shell surya_table DATA_PATH ``` - `DATA_PATH` can be an image, pdf, or folder of images/pdfs - `--images` will save the cropped table images alongside `results.json` (optional) - `--output_dir` specifies the directory to save results to instead of the default - `--page_range` specifies the page range to process in the PDF, specified as a single number, a comma separated list, a range, or comma separated ranges - example: `0,5-10,20`. - `--skip_table_detection` tells table recognition not to detect tables first. Use this if your image is already cropped to a table. The `results.json` file contains a dict keyed by input filename (no extension). Each value is a list of per-table dicts. Each table dict contains: - `html` - full `...
` HTML (including `colspan`, `rowspan`, `		`, ``) - `image_bbox` - the table crop bbox `[0, 0, width, height]` - `error` - true if the table_rec call failed or hit the token cap - `raw` - raw model output, for debugging ### From python ```python from PIL import Image from surya.inference import SuryaInferenceManager from surya.table_rec import TableRecPredictor table_rec_predictor = TableRecPredictor(SuryaInferenceManager()) table_predictions = table_rec_predictor([Image.open(IMAGE_PATH)]) ``` ## Math / equations Surya 2.5 handles math inline as part of OCR — recognized equations come back inside `...` tags in the same HTML output as surrounding prose, in KaTeX-compatible LaTeX. No separate LaTeX OCR pass is needed. ## Output format The model writes each block as a header of special tokens, a label and four coordinates (x0, y0, x1, y1, normalized to 0-1000), followed by the block content: `<|Text|><|120|><|87|><|881|><|255|>

...

`. Tables omit closing tags and mark merged cells with `data-cs` / `data-rs` and `data-kind="parent"` / `"ghost"` spans, which makes pages shorter to write. The `surya-ocr` package decodes all of this for you. If you serve the model yourself, run its output through `surya.inference.parsers.clean_block_html` / `parse_full_page_html`; the lower-level `compact.decode` alone does not convert parent/ghost spans. Your server must return special tokens (llama-server: `--special`). # Inference Backends Layout / OCR / table_rec all share one VLM, served by `vllm` (GPU), `llama.cpp` (CPU / Apple Silicon), or `mlx_vlm` (Apple Silicon). `SuryaInferenceManager` spawns one automatically; you can also point at a pre-running server: ```bash # Attach to an existing vllm or llama-server export SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=vllm export SURYA_INFERENCE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1 export SURYA_INFERENCE_API_KEY=your-api-key # optional ``` | Setting | Default | Notes | |-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------| | `SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND` | auto (vllm if NVIDIA, else llamacpp) | `vllm` \| `llamacpp` \| `mlx` \| unset (auto) | | `SURYA_INFERENCE_URL` | (auto-spawn) | Attach to a running OpenAI-compatible server | | `SURYA_INFERENCE_API_KEY` | `"EMPTY"` (or `VLLM_API_KEY`) | API key for authenticated OpenAI-compatible servers | | `SURYA_CONTAINER_RUNTIME` | auto (`docker` then `podman`) | Container runtime used to launch `vllm/vllm-openai` | | `SURYA_INFERENCE_PARALLEL` | auto (GPU-scaled for vllm, 8 for llamacpp) | Client-side concurrency to the backend | | `SURYA_INFERENCE_KEEP_ALIVE` | false | Leave the spawned server up after exit (cf. `--keep_server`) | | `SURYA_GUIDED_LAYOUT` | true | JSON-schema-constrained layout decode | | `VLLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN` | 24576 | Must hold the largest image (~8k tokens) + prompt + `SURYA_MAX_TOKENS_FULL_PAGE` (12288) | | `VLLM_ENABLE_MTP` | auto | Auto = on only if the checkpoint config declares an MTP head | | `SURYA_MLX_MODEL` | (none) | MLX checkpoint (local dir or HF repo) for `SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=mlx` | | `SURYA_STOP_STRINGS` | (none) | Comma-separated stop strings sent with every request | | `SURYA_STOP_TOKEN_IDS` | (none) | Comma-separated stop token ids (vllm only; ignored by llama.cpp) | | `LLAMA_CPP_SPECIAL` | true | Pass `--special` to llama-server so block labels and coordinates (special tokens in Surya 2.5 output) are returned in the text | ## MLX backend (Apple Silicon) ```bash pip install mlx-vlm==0.7.10 # tested version; experimental backend export SURYA_INFERENCE_BACKEND=mlx export SURYA_MLX_MODEL=/path/to/surya-mlx-int8 # or an HF repo with MLX weights surya_ocr page.png ``` The manager spawns `mlx_vlm.server` for that checkpoint (or attaches to one at `SURYA_INFERENCE_URL`) and uses the same OpenAI-compatible client as the other backends. Auto-detection still picks vllm / llama.cpp; MLX is opt-in. ## Building GGUF and MLX models for a checkpoint ```bash pip install "surya-ocr[build]" # llama.cpp (Metal / CPU / CUDA): writes .gguf and -mmproj.gguf python -m surya.scripts.build_gguf --checkpoint --out-dir ./gguf-build --name --outtype bf16 # MLX (Apple Silicon), optionally quantized (needs `pip install mlx-vlm==0.7.10`) python surya/scripts/build_mlx.py --checkpoint --out-dir ./mlx-build --q-bits 8 ``` Both scripts repair things the stock converters get wrong for the character-level vocabulary: the GGUF script registers the checkpoint's pre-tokenizer hash and, when the Hugging Face tokenizer spells `<|im_end|>` in prompts (Surya 2.5), renames the token's text so llama.cpp tokenizes the prompt the same way; the MLX script restores the original tokenizer files and the end-token id after conversion. # Limitations - Specialized for document OCR and layout analysis. Performance on photos or natural scenes is not the goal. - Requires a running inference backend (`vllm`, `llama-server`, or `mlx_vlm.server`). - For hard documents (handwriting, complex tables, math) or large volumes, the hosted [Datalab API](https://www.datalab.to/?utm_source=gh-surya) uses Chandra and other models, with no infrastructure to manage. ## Troubleshooting If OCR isn't working properly: - Try increasing resolution of the image so the text is bigger (`IMAGE_DPI_HIGHRES=192` or `300`). If the resolution is already very high, `scale_to_fit` automatically downscales images to fit within `3072×2048`. - Preprocessing the image (binarizing, deskewing, etc.) can help with very old/blurry scans. # Manual install If you want to develop Surya locally, install it with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/): ```bash git clone https://github.com/datalab-to/surya.git cd surya uv sync --group dev # installs runtime + dev deps uv run surya_ocr ... # or `source .venv/bin/activate` to enter the venv ``` # Benchmarks Surya 2.5 is a single VLM that handles layout analysis, OCR (full-page or per-block), and table reading in one model. We evaluate end-to-end on two benchmarks: [OmniParseBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench), our open parsing benchmark, and [olmOCR-bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/olmOCR-bench). ## OmniParseBench Headline score (the mean of the text, table and layout scores) against model size for open models. Surya 2.5 scores 85.9 against 83.3 for Surya 2 (both run through this package), in 689M parameters. Scores for the other models are from the [OmniParseBench dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench). | | Headline | Text | Tables | Layout | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Surya 2 | 83.3 | 81.0 | 74.3 | 94.5 | | **Surya 2.5** | **85.9** | **83.8** | **78.3** | **95.7** | Both rows are Surya run through this package at 192 DPI, public scorer, one run per model. The paired differences (Surya 2.5 minus Surya 2, 95% bootstrap interval over pages) are +2.7 [+1.6, +3.7] headline, +2.8 [+1.7, +3.9] text, +4.0 [+1.3, +6.8] tables and +1.2 [+0.3, +2.2] layout. ## olmOCR-bench Surya 2 and Surya 2.5 on the same harness and settings (mean of three passes, plain model output): | Model | Score | |-----------|------:| | Surya 2 | 82.8 | | **Surya 2.5** | **83.7** | Per-source pass rate: | Model | ArXiv | Base | Hdr/Ftr | TinyTxt | MultCol | OldScan | OldMath | Tables | |-----------|------:|-----:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|--------:|-------:| | Surya 2 | 86.7 | 99.7 | 90.7 | 94.4 | 81.3 | 43.2 | 79.0 | 87.4 | | Surya 2.5 | 87.0 | 99.9 | 90.9 | 94.8 | 83.3 | 44.3 | 78.6 | 90.9 | ## Multilingual We also evaluate Surya 2.5 against a 91-language internal benchmark covering text accuracy, layout, tables, math, and reading order in documents drawn from each language. **Overall pass rate: 74.9% across 91 languages (Surya 2: 74.5%),** on a newer, harder version of the benchmark than the 87.2% reported for Surya 2. 21 of the 91 languages score ≥ 90%; 52 score ≥ 80%. Multilingual tables improved (58.1 vs 54.5); text accuracy is level. Tokens per second are about the same; Surya 2.5 writes about a third as many tokens per page. ## Reproducing We score Surya 2.5 on olmOCR-bench by serving the model with `vllm` (or `llama.cpp`) and running the olmOCR-bench harness from [allenai/olmocr](https://github.com/allenai/olmocr), with some adjustments applied to account for our output HTML format. OmniParseBench runs use the Surya adapter in [omni_parse_bench](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench) at 192 DPI. # Training Layout, OCR, and table recognition all share a single vision-language model (Qwen3.5-style architecture, ~690M params). It is trained on diverse document images to emit either a layout JSON or a full-page/block HTML output, depending on prompt.
